title: How to actually code games with AI?
author: HugeShock8
selftext:
I'm a software developer and I have a game idea but I genuinely don't know what I'm doing most of the time. Like game design and everything related to it is very difficult. How can I learn to make a game that actually looks like a game? Because I feel like I got the mechanics somewhat right but it still feels "vibe-coded".

Like just look at it. It doesn't feel like a real game. I've been using MeshyAI for textures and everything but it's too unpolished. I need some tips desperately

replies.author: 314t
replies.body:
Do you want more realism? I would try sites like sketchfab or polyhaven for more realistic free 3d models, your agent can fetch them for you

Ask for sfx that are not procedural generated  
Ask for vfx using shaders, have the agent research instead of hand rolling them from knowledge  
Ask for global illumination lighting, like Godots SDFGI or Unreals lumen, lighting alone makes the game feel better  
Ask for assets that have pbr textures  
Use HDRIs for specific lighting types, you can bake lighting onto assets  
Ask for specific archetypes for characters, or archetypes for other things like a user interface

Just word games with the AI 🙂

comments.author: TennDevStudios
comments.body: What AI models are you using?  Ask Claude or Codex to help make it look the way you want.  Describe the look you want, provide examples and screen shots. comments.author: OWazabi
comments.body:
Maybe some more info on your actual workflow and tools would help.

As a general rule of thumb, for something that doesn't look vibe coded, which is absolutely possible, you need a lot of hand authoring.  
That means polishing every model from meshy, testing and fine tuning every aspect, animation, UI piece, and whatnot.

Obviously, you can do so with the AI, but just telling it to make it look good is not often enough.  
Instead, there's many things you should try and see what fits your workflow best, it's a learning curve to understand how much you can ask from the AI.  
But for example if it's not getting a model right, of the player lets say, you could tell it why you're not liking it, and to start thinking outside of the box, explore different ideas to fix it or improve it, to try various routes and present an artifact with a picker for you to select what approaches work and which don't, letting you type notes in specific places and all, so he gets them and can keep iterating etc.

As a general rule of thumb, you'll get a lot better at everything if you tackle one issue after the other, really finding the right process for it, like a hunt for the right process, that once you have it you can apply it to all of the other models, or projects.

Also if you want good tips, look at this youtube channel : Can it code?  
It's honestly the best, very good concise videos, proper workflows and mentality. You'll thank me later.

comments.author: lawlshawk
comments.body:
I write the design and implementation docs before I let an agent write code.

I came to games from software work too, and I'll spend hours on those docs first. The design lives in them, so the agent is following a plan instead of making one up mid-session.

If yours feels “vibe-coded”, I'd check how many design calls the agent made on its own... those are what I'd move into a doc.
